hints: Look carefully at where the curve flattens out on the right side of the graph. What is the maximum initial rate (Vmax) in mmol s-1?
Remember Km is not a rate, it is a substrate concentration. Find half of Vmax on the y-axis, go across to the curve, then drop straight down to read the substrate concentration on the x-axis.
walkthrough:
**Recall what Km really means**

Think of Km as a measure of affinity. It is defined as the substrate concentration that gives half of the maximum rate.

Key rule:
$$K_m = \text{substrate concentration when rate} = \frac{V_{max}}{2}$$

**Find Vmax from the plateau**

Look at the flat top of the curve where adding more substrate makes no difference. The rate levels off at about $0.38 \text{ mmol s}^{-1}$.

So this is your Vmax:
$$V_{max} \approx 0.38 \text{ mmol s}^{-1}$$

**Halve it and read across and down**

Half of Vmax is about half of 0.38, which is $0.19 \text{ mmol s}^{-1}$.

$$\frac{V_{max}}{2} \approx 0.19 \text{ mmol s}^{-1}$$
Now find 0.19 on the y-axis, move right to the curve, then move straight down to the x-axis. You land at about $1.5 \text{ mmol dm}^{-3}$. That substrate concentration is Km.

options.A: This is the value of half Vmax (0.19 mmol s-1), which is a rate, not a substrate concentration. Km must have units of mmol dm-3.
options.B: This is the value of Vmax itself (0.38 mmol s-1), the maximum rate at the plateau. Km uses half this rate to find the matching substrate concentration.
options.C: Correct. Half Vmax is about 0.19 mmol s-1, and the substrate concentration that gives this rate is about 1.5 mmol dm-3, so Km = 1.5 mmol dm-3.
options.D: At 5.0 mmol dm-3 the enzyme is fully saturated and working at Vmax. Km is found much earlier on the curve, at half Vmax.
